topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Factory Method lets a stable operation request an object while a subclass chooses its concrete type. Worked example: An archive job creates its own record format. ArchiveJob owns a useful stable workflow and exposes one protected virtual creation hook. Concrete jobs select products; the workflow sees only Record.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Identify the workflow that benefits from a creation hook.
Follow product ownership across a factory return.
Distinguish Factory Method from an ordinary factory function.

blocks.text: The creator declares a virtual creation operation returning the product interface. Its ordinary workflow calls that operation and then uses the returned product. A concrete creator overrides the creation operation. The important change is the path of the call: existing workflow code reaches the subclass through virtual dispatch. Moving new into a helper with no overridable creation step does not establish this relationship.

cards.question: What problem does Factory Method address?
cards.answer: Factory Method lets a stable operation request an object while a subclass chooses its concrete type. Worked example: An archive job creates its own record format. ArchiveJob owns a useful stable workflow and exposes one protected virtual creation hook. Concrete jobs select products; the workflow sees only Record.

cards.question: What is Factory Method?
cards.answer: A virtual creation operation called by a creator’s inherited workflow, with concrete creation supplied by derived creators.

cards.question: What is Product?
cards.answer: An object created for another operation to use.

cards.question: What is Simple factory?
cards.answer: A function that selects and constructs a product without requiring an overridable creation hook in a creator hierarchy.

cards.question: If BracketJob overrides make but run directly constructs TextRecord, what prints for sample?
cards.answer: stored text:sample. The workflow bypasses the hook, so the override cannot select BracketRecord.

cards.question: Does returning unique_ptr<Record> from each override remove Factory Method?
cards.answer: No. It changes the ownership contract. Creator inheritance, virtual creation, and product-interface use still define the pattern.

cards.question: A new JSON record needs the same validation and stored prefix. Which two types change?
cards.answer: Add a Record implementation and an ArchiveJob creator that returns it. Keep ArchiveJob::run unchanged so every format still passes the same input gate and prefix step.

cards.question: Why is returning a pointer to a local Record from make unsafe?
cards.answer: The local object dies when make returns. Its address would dangle before run calls format. Return an owning unique_ptr to a separately allocated product instead.

cards.question: Would a switch be simpler for two formats that will never grow?
cards.answer: Yes. A small fixed choice may need only a function and a switch. Factory Method pays for a changing family of creators or a framework-controlled workflow, not for every construction call.

cards.question: Does const on ArchiveJob::run mean no allocation occurs?
cards.answer: No. It prevents ordinary mutation of that job through this method. The method may create and destroy a separate Record, and allocation can still fail.

cards.question: What must a counting mock creator observe for empty input?
cards.answer: Zero calls to make. The text gate runs first. This tests workflow order, which matching one successful output cannot prove.

cards.question: Can replacing unique_ptr with shared_ptr fix a null product?
cards.answer: No. Both smart pointers can be empty. The contract check is still required; shared ownership would change lifetime policy without repairing a missing product.

cards.question: Why retain the EmptyJob negative test when all current real creators are correct?
cards.answer: A future creator can violate the nonnull rule. The test keeps the framework boundary explicit and prevents a later unchecked dereference.

topics.summary: A second integration needs bracketed records. Copying the whole job would copy validation and the stored prefix too. Adding a format switch works for a small closed choice set, but an extensible job family already uses derived types for integration-specific behavior. blocks.text: A product is simply an object made for another part of the program to use. A creator is the object that asks for or makes that product. The Factory Method pattern gives the creator a virtual creation operation. A derived creator decides which concrete product to return. topics.title: Two connected type families, one clear handoff
topics.summary: TextJob and BracketJob derive from ArchiveJob. TextRecord and BracketRecord derive from Record. These are separate relationships. A TextJob is a kind of ArchiveJob; it is not a kind of TextRecord. The job creates the record and then uses it through the Record interface. Confusing those relationships leads to misleading class diagrams and often to bad code.

blocks.text: The protected make declaration returns unique_ptr<Record>. Each override keeps that return type and constructs its concrete class with make_unique. A unique_ptr<TextRecord> can transfer into unique_ptr<Record> when the pointer conversion and deleter requirements are met. This is ownership conversion, not virtual return-type covariance. C++ covariant overrides apply to certain raw pointer and reference return types, not to arbitrary smart-pointer templates.

run receives the owning handle in a local variable. It checks the non-null postcondition, calls format, builds its result string, and leaves scope. The local handle then destroys the product. Returning the string does not extend the product lifetime because the string owns its own characters. If format throws, cleanup still releases the record. The virtual Record destructor is essential for complete destruction through a base owning handle.

topics.title: Compilation fixes the request; execution chooses the maker
topics.summary: The compiler checks that ArchiveJob declares make and that each override matches it. At execution, the object on which run was called determines which make override runs. Calling run through const ArchiveJob& selected still reaches BracketJob::make when selected refers to the bracket job. A reference changes what operations the caller can name; it does not erase the actual object type.

blocks.text: The call to make happens after label validation. An empty or oversized label therefore creates no product. Once a product exists, its format method is another virtual call. The sequence is shared validation, virtual creation, virtual formatting, then shared receipt assembly. Factory Method is often one specialized step inside a Template Method-style workflow, but the terms describe different decisions: one concerns object creation; the other concerns algorithm order.

A null result is a broken creator contract, so the job throws logic_error. EmptyJob exists only to verify that guard. An allocation failure can also occur inside make_unique and propagate as an exception; no successfully constructed handle exists to leak. For a real file-backed product, document whether creation opens a file, delays opening, or can reuse a resource. The pattern alone says nothing about those effects.

topics.title: What does not make a Factory Method
topics.summary: A free function make_record(format) with a switch is commonly called a simple factory. It centralizes construction and may be exactly what a program needs. It is not this pattern’s defining mechanism because no inherited workflow calls an overridable creation hook. A static member named create is not automatically Factory Method either. Names do not decide a design pattern; relationships and control flow do.

blocks.text: If the caller can supply a ready-made Record, dependency injection is often simpler than subclassing ArchiveJob. If the workflow needs a fresh record for every run, it can accept a callable factory. Factory Method fits best when creator inheritance already has a clear role and subclasses should choose products. Avoid introducing two class hierarchies solely to hide one constructor.

New product behavior still needs interface-level tests. A new format that silently truncates labels could satisfy the C++ signature and still violate requirements. Likewise, switching the product does not make the stored prefix truthful about persistent storage. Keep the workflow’s externally promised behavior explicit, and test it through the base creator interface so extensions exercise the same path clients will use.

items: run validates before it calls make.

blocks.text: Alternative: A simple factory function plus an ordinary workflow is smaller for a closed list of formats. Injecting a factory callable avoids creator inheritance when object creation varies independently of job type.

topics.title: Exercise 01.4: Choose a design
topics.summary: A program has a switch selecting two record types, with no useful creator inheritance. Should the team add a base creator just to claim Factory Method? Explain a smaller design.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: A pattern name is not a requirement.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Keep a simple factory function returning unique_ptr<Record>, or pass a ready-made record when its lifetime fits. Add inherited creation only when a shared creator workflow genuinely benefits from subclass choices. The smaller design centralizes construction with fewer relationships to maintain.

cards.question: A program has a switch selecting two record types, with no useful creator inheritance. Should the team add a base creator just to claim Factory Method? Explain a smaller design.
cards.answer: Keep a simple factory function returning unique_ptr<Record>, or pass a ready-made record when its lifetime fits. Add inherited creation only when a shared creator workflow genuinely benefits from subclass choices. The smaller design centralizes construction with fewer relationships to maintain.

topics.title: Exercise 01.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A reviewer asks why make returns unique_ptr<Record> instead of Record&. Explain the lifetime difference and a valid use for borrowing.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Who destroys the created record?

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: The current contract creates a fresh record owned by run, so unique_ptr states who destroys it even when formatting throws. A reference would need a separate owner that outlives the call, such as a cached immutable product stored in the creator. Borrowing is reasonable under that different lifetime contract, but returning a reference to a local record is invalid.

blocks.title: Main points
items: Factory Method varies construction through an inherited virtual hook.
The creator must have a reason to exist beyond renaming a constructor.
Product and creator inheritance are separate relationships.
Return ownership clearly and validate required non-null products.
A free factory function is often a useful simpler design.

concepts.definition: A virtual creation operation called by a creator’s inherited workflow, with concrete creation supplied by derived creators.
An object created for another operation to use.
A function that selects and constructs a product without requiring an overridable creation hook in a creator hierarchy.

discussion.question: A program has a switch selecting two record types, with no useful creator inheritance. Should the team add a base creator just to claim Factory Method? Explain a smaller design.
discussion.answer: Keep a simple factory function returning unique_ptr<Record>, or pass a ready-made record when its lifetime fits. Add inherited creation only when a shared creator workflow genuinely benefits from subclass choices. The smaller design centralizes construction with fewer relationships to maintain.
discussion.hint: A pattern name is not a requirement.

workshop.alternative: A simple factory function plus an ordinary workflow is smaller for a closed list of formats. Injecting a factory callable avoids creator inheritance when object creation varies independently of job type.
workshop.design: ArchiveJob owns a useful stable workflow and exposes one protected virtual creation hook. Concrete jobs select products; the workflow sees only Record.
invariants: run validates before it calls make.
A successful make returns a non-null owning handle.
The receipt preserves the entire accepted label in the selected format.
workshop.maintenance: A format extension adds a product and a matching creator without copying label checks. Review whether creator inheritance remains useful as integrations grow; a factory callable can become clearer when combinations multiply.
workshop.verification: main checks both receipt formats through direct and base-reference calls, accepts exactly 20 bytes, rejects 0 and 21 bytes, and checks a null-returning creator. These tests cover the string workflow, not disk persistence or allocation-failure injection.
